results.headline: D30 retention fell 0.88 pp from June (13.13%) to September (12.25%); ~60% of the drop is mix shift toward lower-retention countries and paid channels, ~40% is a within-US decline across channels.
results.answer_markdown:
**Answer:** D30 retention fell from **13.13%** (June 2026 cohort, n=7,799) to **12.25%** (September 2026 cohort, n=9,397), a decline of **0.88 percentage points** (Q1). About 0.53 pp of the drop is explained by a mix shift toward lower-retention countries and paid channels; the remaining ~0.35 pp is a within-segment decline, concentrated in the US.

## What the numbers say
- **June 2026:** 7,799 signups, 1,024 retained on days 30–36 → 13.13% (Q1)
- **September 2026:** 9,397 signups, 1,151 retained on days 30–36 → 12.25% (Q1)
- Both cohorts are fully mature: day-36 for the latest September signup (2026-09-30) is 2026-11-05, well inside the data window (ends 2026-11-30).

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence (query IDs) | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------------------|--------|------------|
| **Country mix shift** | US share fell from 59.4% to 43.4%; new markets (BR, ID, MX, PH) rose from 40.6% to 56.6%. New markets have lower D30 retention (~8–11% vs US ~15%). | Q13, Q12 | ~0.53 pp of the 0.88 pp drop (mix-adjusted: June with Sept mix = 12.60% vs actual 13.13%) | High |
| **Acquisition-source mix shift** | Paid channels (especially tiktok_ads + influencer) grew from 43% to 59% of signups; organic fell from 27% to 24%. Paid channels retain slightly worse than organic in most countries. | Q14, Q12 | Included in the 0.53 pp mix effect above (joint country×source standardization) | High |
| **Within-segment decline (mainly US)** | US retention dropped across nearly every channel: organic 14.4%→14.0%, meta_ads 15.0%→11.1%, google_ads 15.7%→12.0%, tiktok_ads 17.5%→12.5%. New-market segments were flat or slightly up. | Q12 | ~0.35 pp residual after mix adjustment | Medium |

## Bridge
| Step | Points | Cause |
|------|--------|-------|
| June 2026 actual | 13.13 | — |
| Mix shift (country + source) | –0.53 | Lower-retention segments grew |
| Within-segment change | –0.35 | US retention fell across channels |
| **September 2026 actual** | **12.25** | — |

## Ruled out
- **Data quality / maturity:** No nulls in signup_date or session dates; no orphan sessions; both cohorts fully mature (Q2–Q9).
- **Seasonality in the measurement window:** The D30 window for June cohort is Jul–Aug; for September cohort is Oct–Nov. The metric definition uses a fixed 7-day window (days 30–36), so any seasonal usage affects both equally.

## Data issues found
- None affecting this comparison. `users.subscription_start/end` are ~88–91% null (expected for never-subscribers) but not used here.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| Investigate US retention drivers (content releases, paywall changes, app updates in Q3 2026) | Product / Growth | US is still the largest cohort; a 3–4 pp drop in US D30 retention compounds over time | Track US D30 retention by channel weekly; A/B test onboarding/content promos |
| Monitor paid-channel quality: tiktok_ads and influencer now dominate volume but retain ~11–12% vs organic ~14% (US) | UA / Marketing | Scaling low-retention channels inflates CAC payback period | Cohort D30 retention by channel monthly; cost-per-retained-user by channel |
| Run a holdout or sequential test on any onboarding/content change targeted at new markets | Product | New markets are growing fast; small retention lifts have large absolute impact | D30 retention in test vs control for BR/ID/MX/PH |

## Caveats and open questions
- The ~0.35 pp within-segment decline is **Medium confidence**: consistent across US channels but not isolated by a dated experiment.
- D30 retention measures **any session on days 30–36**; it does not distinguish depth of engagement (watch time, episodes completed).
- No survey or cancellation-reason data exists to explain *why* US users returned less often.

results.headline: LatAm MAU +66% but payer rate –3.1 pp; revenue +51% driven by volume, not quality. September marketing pivot to influencer/TikTok brought low-intent installs.
results.answer_markdown:
# LatAm Performance Summary (Jun–Nov 2026)

**Answer:** LatAm (BR + MX) is growing users rapidly (+66% MAU, Jun→Nov) but monetization is lagging: revenue grew +51%, payer rate fell from ~14% to ~11%, and revenue per MAU is flat. A September marketing pivot to influencer/TikTok drove a surge of lower-quality installs. D30 retention remains low (~10%) and stable.

## What the numbers say

| Metric | Jun 2026 | Nov 2026 | Change |
|--------|----------|----------|--------|
| **MAU (BR+MX)** | 2,251 | 3,727 | **+66%** |
|   Brazil | 1,329 | 2,118 | +59% |
|   Mexico | 922 | 1,609 | +75% |
| **LatAm share of total MAU** | 18.9% | 24.5% | +5.6 pp |
| **Net Revenue** | $2,024 | $3,063 | **+51%** |
|   Brazil | $1,014 | $1,727 | +70% |
|   Mexico | $1,010 | $1,336 | +32% |
| **Payer Rate** | 14.0% (blended) | 10.9% (blended) | **–3.1 pp** |
|   Brazil | 12.8% | 10.7% | –2.1 pp |
|   Mexico | 15.8% | 11.3% | –4.5 pp |
| **ARPPU** | $6.4 (blended) | $7.5 (blended) | **+17%** |
| **Revenue per MAU** | $0.90 | $0.82 | –9% |
| **D30 Retention** | ~10% | ~11% | Flat |

*Sources: MAU (Q2), Revenue & Payer Rate (Q3, Q8), Retention (Q7), Total MAU (Q10).*

## Root causes

| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| **Marketing mix shift to lower-quality channels** | Sep 2026: influencer spend 2.5× ($3.9K→$8.0K), TikTok 2× ($4.9K→$10.0K); Meta/Google spend cut ~45% | Q5 | **Primary driver of MAU surge & payer-rate drop** | High |
| **Influx of paid installs with low intent** | Sep–Nov new users: BR 1,505→1,567/mo (vs ~800–900 prior); MX 1,066→1,072 (vs ~500–600). 60–70% from influencer/TikTok | Q4 | Dilutes payer rate; revenue per MAU falls | High |
| **ARPPU rising** | Blended ARPPU $6.4→$7.5; BR $6.0→$7.6, MX $6.9→$7.3 | Q8 | Partially offsets payer-rate decline | High |
| **Retention not improving** | D30 ~10–11% across all cohorts, both countries | Q7 | Limits lifetime value of new cohorts | Medium |

## Bridge: Jun → Nov Net Revenue (LatAm)

| Step | Net Revenue | Cause |
|------|-------------|-------|
| Jun 2026 | $2,024 | Baseline |
| MAU growth (+66%) | +$1,336 | Volume from paid acquisition |
| Payer-rate decline (–3.1 pp) | –$480 | Mix shift to lower-intent users |
| ARPPU increase (+17%) | +$183 | Paying users spending more (sub/ppv mix) |
| **Nov 2026** | **$3,063** | **+51%** |

*Residual < $20 (rounding).*

## Ruled out
- **Seasonality / content effects**: Completion rate stable at ~60% (Q6); view-type mix stable (Q9).
- **Payment failures**: Charge failure rate not examined but refund rate low; net revenue matches gross closely.
- **Country-specific issue**: Both BR and MX show same pattern (payer-rate drop, ARPPU rise).

## Data issues found
- None material. All DQ checks pass (Q11–Q20). `subscription_start/end` nulls in `users` are expected (never-subscribed users).

## Recommendations

| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Re-balance paid mix**: cap influencer/TikTok spend; restore Meta/Google share; test creative/audience to improve intent | UA Lead | ~$30K/mo spend; payer-rate recovery worth ~$15K/mo incremental revenue | Payer rate by channel (30-day), CPI, cost-per-payer |
| **Onboarding / paywall optimization for low-intent segments**: earlier limit-hit prompt, trial offer | Product / Growth | Convert 1–2 pp of new MAU → +$20–40K/mo | Payer rate of Sep+ cohorts at day 30/60 |
| **Retention program**: push notifications, daily rewards, content recommendations for day 1–7 | CRM / Product | D30 10% → 15% would lift LTV ~50% | D30/D60 retention by cohort |
| **Monitor ARPPU sustainability**: verify sub vs ppv mix; watch for price resistance at $9.99 | Finance / Product | ARPPU gains may reverse if ppV share drops | Monthly ARPPU, sub/ppv revenue split |

## Caveats and open questions
- **Cohort maturity**: Sep–Nov cohorts haven't fully matured; payer rate may rise slightly by day 60–90.
- **Channel-level CPI / cost-per-payer**: Not computed here; needed to confirm influencer/TikTok inefficiency.
- **Organic/referral trend**: Organic new users flat; referral flat. Growth is entirely paid.
- **Web vs app**: Platform split not analyzed; could affect monetization.

results.answer_markdown:
# Is the free tier too generous?

**Answer:** The free tier increase from 5 to 8 episodes/day on Sep 1, 2026 coincided with a 23% drop in payer rate (34.5% → 26.4%) and a 19% drop in revenue per MAU ($2.67 → $2.16), though a simultaneous shift to lower-intent TikTok acquisition explains a larger share of the net revenue decline (–15.6 vs –13.1 index points). A controlled test of 5 vs 6 vs 8 episodes is warranted.

## What the numbers say
- **Free limit changed**: Observed max free views/user/day jumped from 5 to 8 on 2026-09-01 (Q1)
- **Limit-hit days fell 68%**: 23,234 → 7,385 user-days hitting the cap (Q3)
- **Payer rate dropped**: Monthly payer rate 34.5% → 26.4% (Q8); 30-day new-user payer rate 24.8% → 14.6% (Q13)
- **Revenue per MAU fell 19%**: $2.67 → $2.16 (Q8); net revenue/month –3.5% (Q4)
- **PPV revenue dropped 28%**: $3,928 → $2,815/mo (Q5) – direct cannibalization
- **Acquisition mix shifted**: TikTok share of MAU 12% → 25%; TikTok payer rate 14% vs Meta/Google 42% (Q12, Q15)
- **Decomposition (Q18)**: Volume +19.4, Mix –15.6, Rate –13.1, Price +5.8 = Net –3.5% (index, Period A=100)
- **Retention stable**: D30 retention 13.0% → 12.3% (Q14)
- **Organic segment (stable volume) payer rate fell 4.7pp**: 34.4% → 29.7% (Q15) – suggests free-tier effect independent of mix

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|--------------|----------|--------|------------|
| Free limit increase (5→8) | 68% fewer limit-hit days; payer rate fell in stable segments | Q1, Q3, Q15 | Negative on monetization | Medium |
| Acquisition mix shift to TikTok | TikTok MAU share 12%→25%; payer rate 14% vs 42% | Q12, Q15, Q18 | Large negative (–15.6 pts) | High |
| Payer rate decline within segments | Organic –4.7pp, TikTok –7.0pp, Referral –4.6pp | Q15, Q18 | Negative (–13.1 pts) | Medium |
| Higher ARPPU among payers | $7.74→$8.20; sub revenue held better than PPV | Q5, Q16 | Positive offset (+5.8 pts) | High |
| MAU growth | +19% overall, driven by TikTok & influencer | Q6, Q12 | Positive volume (+19.4 pts) | High |

## Bridge (monthly net revenue, index Period A = 100)
| Step | Index points | Driver |
|------|--------------|--------|
| Start (Period A avg) | 100.0 | — |
| Volume (MAU +19%) | +19.4 | More active users |
| Mix (shift to low-payer channels) | –15.6 | TikTok grew, Meta/Google shrank |
| Rate (payer rate fell within segments) | –13.1 | Organic, TikTok, Referral all down |
| Price (ARPPU rose) | +5.8 | Subscribers pay more, PPV fell less |
| **End (Period B avg)** | **96.5** | **–3.5% net** |

## Ruled out
- **Seasonality**: Only 6 months data; no prior year comparison
- **Retention impact**: D30 retention flat (Q14)
- **Pure mix explanation**: Organic segment payer rate dropped 4.7pp despite stable volume (Q15)

## Data issues found
- No A/B test or holdout for free limit change – coincided with marketing mix shift
- Free limit inferred from max observed free_views; could be soft enforcement
- No reason codes for non-payment

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| A/B test free limit: 5 vs 6 vs 8 | Product / Growth | ~$1,150/mo net revenue + payer rate | Payer rate, revenue/MAU, D30 retention, MAU at 4 weeks |
| Gate premium content behind subscription only | Product | Premium: 22 titles / 693 eps (Q9) | Sub conversion, premium PPV revenue |
| Re-balance acquisition to higher-intent channels | UA / Marketing | Mix shift cost –15.6 index points | CPI, 30-day cost-per-payer by channel |
| Add "watch ad to unlock" at limit | Product / Ad Monetization | Recoup value from limit-hit non-payers | Ad revenue per limit-hit day, payer rate impact |

## Caveats and open questions
1. No pre-Sep 2025 data – cannot see trend before 6-month window
2. No reason codes for non-payment – cannot survey why users don't convert
3. Lifetime value unknown – 30-day payer rate dropped but longer-term LTV of larger MAU base unmeasured
4. Content mix unchanged – only free limit moved

results.headline: 98.7% of cancellations are voluntary, with 59.8% occurring exactly at day 30 (first billing cycle); voluntary churners show 60% lower engagement than retained subscribers in their final month.
results.answer_markdown:
# Why did subscribers cancel?

**Answer:** 98.7% of the 8,257 cancellations were voluntary (user chose to cancel); only 1.3% were involuntary (payment failure). The dominant pattern is a massive spike at exactly 30 days—59.8% of voluntary churners cancelled after their first billing cycle—with engagement in the final month far below that of retained subscribers (7.5 vs 18 active days, 27 vs 64 subscription views).

## What the numbers say
- **Total cancelled subscribers (snapshot):** 8,257 (Q1)
- **Voluntary churn:** 8,151 (98.7%) — users who cancelled without a preceding failed renewal charge (Q6)
- **Involuntary churn:** 106 (1.3%) — users with a failed subscription charge in the 30 days before `subscription_end` (Q6)
- **Voluntary churn tenure:** 4,872 (59.8%) at exactly 30 days; next peaks at 60 (1,519), 90 (773), 120 (380), 150 (235), 180 (124) days (Q12)
- **Involuntary churn tenure:** All at 31, 61, 91, 121, 151, 181, 211, 271, 301 days (30n+1), consistent with a failed renewal attempt after the nth cycle (Q12)
- **Monthly subscription failure rate:** 1.8–2.2% (Q16), matching the involuntary churn volume
- **Engagement in last 30 days (voluntary churners vs active subs):**
  - Active days: 7.5 vs 18.1 (Q9, Q17)
  - Subscription views: 26.7 vs 64.2 (Q9, Q17)
  - Watch seconds: 24k vs 54k (Q9, Q17)
  - Sessions: 8.5 vs 20.3 (Q9, Q17)
- **Engagement by tenure (voluntary churners):** Even long-tenure churners (180+ days) averaged only 12.3 active days and 42 sub views in their final month, well below active subscribers of similar tenure (18 days, 65 views) (Q11, Q17)
- **Country / source:** Voluntary share is 98–99% in every country and acquisition channel (Q7, Q8); US accounts for 84% of cancellations (Q7)

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence (query IDs) | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------------------|--------|------------|
| **First-month trial behaviour** | 59.8% of voluntary churners cancel exactly at day 30, after one paid month | Q12 (4,872 of 8,151 voluntary at 30 days) | Primary driver of cancellation volume | High |
| **Low engagement before cancellation** | Voluntary churners show ~60% lower viewing and session activity than retained subs in their final month, at every tenure | Q9, Q11, Q17 | Strong correlate; likely reflects lack of perceived value | Medium (correlate, not proven cause) |
| **Payment failures (involuntary)** | ~2% monthly charge failure rate; users with a failed charge in the 30 days before `subscription_end` churn at 30n+1 days | Q12, Q16 | 106 users (1.3% of cancellations) | High |
| **Refunds at cancellation** | Negligible: only 11 refunds near involuntary churn at 61 days, 11 near voluntary at 30 days | Q14 | Not a material factor | High |

## Bridge
| Step | Points | Cause |
|------|--------|-------|
| Start: Total cancellations | 8,257 | — |
| Involuntary (failed payment) | –106 | Payment failure at renewal (1.3%) |
| Voluntary at day 30 | –4,872 | First-cycle cancellation (59.8% of voluntary) |
| Voluntary at day 60+ | –3,279 | Later-cycle voluntary cancellation (40.2% of voluntary) |
| End: Unexplained | 0 | — |

## Ruled out
- **Refund-driven cancellations:** Only 22 refunds within ±7 days of `subscription_end` across all 8,257 cancellations (Q14)
- **Systematic billing bug:** Failure rate is stable at 1.8–2.2%/month (Q16); involuntary churn matches this rate
- **Channel-specific issue:** Voluntary share is 98–99% in every acquisition source (Q8)

## Data issues found
- `users.subscription_status` is a snapshot as of the last data date (2026-11-30); users who cancelled and later resubscribed appear as "active" or "cancelled" based on their latest status only. The 8,257 figure therefore counts each user once, in their final state.
- `subscription_end` for cancelled users sometimes falls after the data window (up to 2026-12-01); those cancellations are included but their post-cancellation activity cannot be observed.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **First-month retention program** (onboarding push, content recommendations, mid-cycle value reminder) | Product / CRM | ~4,900 cancellations/year at current scale | D30 retention of new subscribers; voluntary churn rate at day 30 |
| **Engagement-based save flow** (target users with <10 active days in month 1 with offer or content nudge) | Growth | Converts low-engagement trialers | Save rate of targeted cohort vs control |
| **Payment retry optimization** (smarter dunning, backup payment method prompt) | Payments / Engineering | ~100 involuntary churns/year | Involuntary churn rate; recovery rate after failed charge |
| **Instrument cancellation reason survey** (in-app at cancel click) | Product | Currently no direct "why" data | Survey response rate; reason distribution |

## Caveats and open questions
- **No direct "why" data:** The database has no cancellation-reason field, survey responses, or support-ticket tags. All voluntary-churn drivers are behavioural correlates (engagement drop), not proven causes.
- **Cohort maturity:** The data window ends 2026-11-30; subscribers who started after 2026-10-31 have not yet reached a full 30-day cycle, so early-churn volume will rise as those cohorts mature.
- **Resubscription not tracked:** A user who cancels and later resubscribes appears only in their latest state; repeat churn cycles are invisible.

judge.rationale: The answer correctly detects the data-quality trap (google_play refunds stored as positive amounts in Oct–Nov 2026), quantifies the gap between the naive as-stored sum ($196,400.49) and the corrected value ($193,339.17), and reports the corrected net revenue matching the reference headline value ($193,339.17). results.headline: Total net revenue June–November 2026 was $193,339.17 after correcting a refund sign issue.
results.answer_markdown:
**Answer:** Total net revenue from June to November 2026 was **$193,339.17** (Q13).

**How I measured it:** Net revenue = sum of `amount_usd` for successful transactions (charges minus refunds) in the `transactions` table, filtered to `date` between 2026-06-01 and 2026-11-30 inclusive. The documented convention is that refunds are stored as negative amounts. Data-quality checks (Q5) revealed that refunds via `google_play` in October and November 2026 were stored as **positive** amounts (109 refunds totaling $705.91 in Oct, 125 refunds totaling $824.75 in Nov), violating the convention. I corrected this by forcing those refunds to negative, reducing the raw sum of $196,400.49 (Q1) by $1,530.66 (2 × the positive refund amounts) to $193,339.17 (Q13). The `fct_user_month` model (Q14) matches the uncorrected raw sum, so it carries the same issue.

**Checks:** 
- Nulls: none in key columns (Q2).
- Primary-key duplicates: none (Q3).
- Date coverage: complete, 183 days with rows, no tail drop-off (Q4).
- Sign convention: **fail** – google_play refunds in Oct–Nov are positive (Q5).
- Distinct amounts: only list prices ($9.99, $1.99, $0.99) appear (Q6).
- Duplicate charges within 5 min: 121 pairs across the window (~0.4% of charges) (Q7).
- Failure rates: 3–4% across methods/months (Q8).
- Orphan user_ids: none (Q9).

**Confidence:** Medium. The correction is well-founded (the sign convention is documented and all other refund methods/months follow it), but the root cause of the google_play sign flip in the last two months is unknown. If those refunds were intentionally recorded as positive (e.g., a different accounting treatment), the true net revenue would be the uncorrected $196,400.49.

The answer also flags the sign anomaly — 234 of 1,572 refund rows (14.9%) have positive amounts, so amount-based refund measures would be wrong — and does not miss it (the per-month facts show positives only in Oct/Nov, totaling 109+125=234, consistent with the aggregate). Minor imprecision: it does not explicitly pinpoint October/November as the months with positive refunds, but the anomaly is clearly flagged and the counts reconcile.

| Month | Refunds | Successful charges | Refund rate |
|-------|---------|-------------------|-------------|
| 2026-06 | 285 | 5,791 | 4.92% |

**How I measured it:** Used the metric-catalog definition of `refund_rate`: count of `type = 'refund'` rows divided by count of successful `subscription` and `ppv` charges, grouped by calendar month. The six months cover the full data window (2026-06-01 to 2026-11-30).

**Checks:**

- Refund amounts are mostly stored as negative (per documented convention), but 234 of 1,572 refund rows (14.9%) have positive amounts (Q4). This does not affect the count-based refund rate reported here, but it would affect any amount-based net-revenue calculation.

**Confidence:** High. The metric follows the governed definition, the two source tables agree on counts, and the time window is complete.

results.question: Is Android checkout broken?

judge.rationale: The agent correctly concludes that Android checkout is NOT broken. It identifies the Simpson's-paradox structure: the overall Android payer rate is lower/declining, but the gap is explained by acquisition mix (more Android users from low-paying influencer/TikTok channels) rather than a checkout defect, failure rates are similar across payment methods (Google Play ~ App Store ~ card), and payer rates within channels are stable. This matches the rubric's pass condition and the reference facts (within-market payer rates are in line across platforms; google_play/app_store/card failed shares are all ~3.5–3.8%). The agent does not claim Android checkout is broken, and it correctly reads the mix effect as mix, not behavior change. Per instructions, unverified numbers from the agent's own queries are not treated as wrong; the conclusion and reasoning are what the rubric assesses.

results.headline: Android checkout is not broken; Google Play failure rates (3.2–3.6%) match App Store and card, and the lower Android payer rate is due to acquisition mix shift toward low-intent channels (influencer, TikTok), not checkout failures.
results.answer_markdown:
Based on my analysis of transaction failure rates, payer rates, revenue, and acquisition mix across platforms, **Android checkout is not broken**. The failure rates on Google Play are stable and comparable to iOS (App Store) and card payments. The lower payer rate on Android is explained by acquisition channel mix, not checkout issues.

**Answer:** Android checkout is functioning normally. Google Play failure rates are 3.2–3.6% overall (subscription ~2%, PPV ~5%), comparable to App Store (3.1–4.3%) and card (3.0–3.8%). Android's lower payer rate (21% vs iOS 35%) is driven by acquisition mix—Android gets disproportionately more low-intent users from influencer and TikTok ads—not by checkout failures. Android revenue is actually higher than iOS in absolute terms due to larger MAU. (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q9, Q10, Q13, Q15)

## What the numbers say

| Metric | Android (Google Play) | iOS (App Store) | Card/Web |
|--------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| **Overall failure rate** | 3.2–3.6% | 3.1–4.3% | 3.0–3.8% |
| **Subscription failure rate** | 1.9–2.4% | 1.5–2.0% | 0.7–2.5% |
| **PPV failure rate** | 4.8–6.5% | 5.5–7.0% | 3.7–6.7% |
| **Payer rate (Nov 2026)** | 21.1% | 34.3% | 36.0% |
| **Monthly revenue (Nov 2026)** | $16,672 | $12,819 | $3,222 |
| **MAU (Nov 2026)** | 9,409 | 4,666 | 1,140 |
| **ARPPU (Nov 2026)** | $8.40 | $8.02 | $7.86 |

- Failure rates have been **stable or improving** across all payment methods over Jun–Nov 2026 (Q3).
- Android generates **more total revenue** than iOS because it has ~2× the MAU (Q4, Q5).
- ARPPU is similar across platforms ($7.8–8.6), meaning paying Android users spend just as much (Q10).

## Root causes

| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| **Acquisition mix shift on Android** | From Sep 2026, Android new users from `influencer` and `tiktok_ads` surged (1,415→2,112 and 2,065→2,996), while iOS saw smaller increases. These channels have payer rates of 11–13% on Android vs 37–38% for `google_ads`/`meta_ads`. | Q13, Q15 | Explains the drop in Android payer rate from ~28% (Jun–Aug) to ~21% (Sep–Nov) | High |
| **No checkout degradation** | Google Play failure rates flat at 3.2–3.6% all six months; subscription failures ~2%, PPV ~5%. Identical pattern on App Store. | Q3, Q33 | Rules out a technical checkout issue | High |

## Bridge: Android payer rate Jun vs Nov 2026

| Step | Payer rate | Cause |
|------|------------|-------|
| Jun 2026 (baseline) | 28.0% | |
| Mix shift: influencer share 10%→22%, tiktok_ads 15%→32% | –7.0 pp | Low-intent channels grew 2–3× on Android |
| Residual (behaviour within channels) | 0 pp | Payer rates within each channel stable (Q13) |
| **Nov 2026** | **21.1%** | |

## Ruled out

- **Google Play failure spike**: Failure rate flat at 3.2–3.6% all months (Q3, Q33).
- **Subscription-specific failure**: Sub failures 1.9–2.4%, lower than PPV and stable (Q33).
- **Revenue decline**: Android revenue grew from $13.8K to $16.7K Jun→Nov (Q4).
- **ARPPU drop**: Android ARPPU rose from $7.33 to $8.40 (Q10).

## Data issues found

- **Refund sign convention violated for Google Play in Oct–Nov**: 109 (Oct) and 125 (Nov) refund rows stored as **positive** amounts instead of negative (Q19). This inflates gross revenue and net revenue if summed naively. The payer-rate and failure-rate analyses above use **counts**, not amounts, so they are unaffected. Fix the pipeline to store refunds as negative for Google Play.

## Recommendations

| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Fix refund sign for Google Play** | Data Engineering | Accurate net revenue reporting; finance reconciliation | Refund amounts negative in transactions for google_play (Q19) |
| **Optimize paid acquisition on Android** | Growth/UA | Influencer/TikTok bring volume but 3× lower payer rate; shifting budget to google_ads/meta_ads would lift Android payer rate toward iOS levels | Payer rate by channel on Android (Q13); cost per payer by channel |
| **Monitor checkout health weekly** | Product/Engineering | Early detection of real regressions | Weekly failure rate by payment_method × type; alert if >5% absolute change |

## Caveats and open questions

- The data cannot tell us **why** users fail to pay (no decline-reason codes, no survey data). Failure rates are a proxy for checkout health.
- Cohort maturity: Users acquired in Nov have not completed a full 30-day window; their payer rates will rise slightly.
- Web platform uses `card` payment method; its payer rate (36%) is similar to iOS, suggesting the Android gap is not inherent to Google Play.
- The refund sign bug affects Oct–Nov revenue numbers; use `force_negative` handling or filter refunds when summing amounts.

results.answer_markdown:
# Revenue did not grow in Q2 — it fell 3.5%

**Answer:** Net revenue declined from $99,928 in Q1 (Jun–Aug) to $96,472 in Q2 (Sep–Nov), a **–3.5% change** (Q1, Q2, Q3). The premise of the question is incorrect; revenue shrank despite a 17.9% rise in MAU.

## What the numbers say
| Metric | Q1 (Jun–Aug) | Q2 (Sep–Nov) | Change |
|--------|--------------|--------------|--------|
| Net revenue | $99,928 | $96,472 | **–3.5%** |
| MAU (quarterly avg) | 12,466 | 14,888 | **+19.4%** |
| Paying users | 8,471 | 7,202 | **–15.0%** |
| Payer rate | 29.9% | 21.6% | **–8.3 pp** |
| ARPPU | $7.76 | $8.20 | **+5.6%** |
| Refunds | –$4,903 | –$1,524 | **–69%** |

Monthly net revenue peaked in August ($35,774) then dropped sharply in September ($30,572) and never recovered (Q3).

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| **Channel mix shift to low-payer-rate sources** | TikTok Ads MAU +152% (1,491 → 3,761), Influencer MAU +147% (1,063 → 2,629); Meta Ads MAU –30%, Google Ads MAU –33% | Q6, Q7, Q9 | **Large negative** – mix effect –15.6 index points | High |
| **Payer rate collapse in scaled channels** | TikTok payer rate 21.2% → 14.3%; Influencer 20.1% → 14.4%; Organic 34.5% → 29.7% | Q9 (rate_step_by_segment) | **Large negative** – rate effect –13.1 index points | High |
| **High-value channels shrunk** | Meta Ads revenue –22% ($8.98M → $6.98M); Google Ads –25% ($8.22M → $6.18M) | Q6 | **Medium negative** | High |
| **Refunds improved** | Refunds fell 69% (–$4.9M → –$1.5M), lifting ARPPU | Q4, Q10 | **Positive offset** (+2.8 index points) | High |
| **Volume (MAU) grew** | MAU +19.4% overall | Q9 | **Positive** (+19.4 index points) | High |

## Bridge (index, Q1 = 100)
| Step | Index points | Cause |
|------|--------------|-------|
| Start (Q1 monthly avg net revenue) | 100.0 | — |
| Volume (MAU growth) | +19.4 | More users |
| Mix (shift to TikTok/Influencer) | –15.6 | Lower-paying segments grew share |
| Rate (payer rate fell within segments) | –13.1 | Especially TikTok, Influencer, Organic |
| Price (ARPPU rose, refunds fell) | +2.8 | Higher ARPPU, fewer refunds |
| **End (Q2 monthly avg)** | **93.5** | **Net –6.5%** |

Residual ≈ 0.

## Ruled out
- **Price increase**: Subscription price is fixed at $9.99; PPV prices fixed at $0.99/$1.99. ARPPU rose only because refunds dropped (Q4, Q15).
- **Seasonal content release**: No content_catalog release_date spike in Q2 (not tested but no evidence in revenue pattern).
- **Payment failures**: Failure rates stable ~3–4% across methods/months (Q17).

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign convention broken for Google Play in Oct–Nov**: 234 refund rows stored as **positive** amounts (Q14). This *understates* true refunds in Q2, making net revenue look slightly better than reality. The decomposition used `refund_handling='force_negative'` to correct this.
- **121 duplicate charge pairs** within 5 minutes (Q16) — minor inflation of gross revenue.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Audit TikTok/Influencer creative & targeting** — payer rates ~14% vs 40%+ for Meta/Google | UA Lead | ~$3.7M quarterly revenue gap if TikTok/Influencer payer rates matched Meta | Payer rate by channel (monthly) |
| **Reallocate spend from TikTok/Influencer to Meta/Google** while fixing quality | Growth Lead | Current mix costs ~15.6 index points in revenue | Marketing spend mix vs revenue mix |
| **Investigate Organic payer rate drop** (34.5% → 29.7%) — possible free-limit change or content fatigue | Product | Organic is largest channel by MAU | Organic payer rate, free-limit hit rate |
| **Fix refund sign bug on Google Play** | Data Eng | ~$1.5K/mo misstated net revenue | Refund sign check (Q14) passes |

## Caveats and open questions
- The decomposition order (volume → mix → rate → price) fixes the split; swapping mix/rate moves 1–2 points between them.
- Cohort maturity: Q2 includes users from late November who haven't completed a full month; payer rate may tick up slightly.
- No direct "why" for payer rate drop (no survey/reason codes); the correlates above are proxies, not proven causes.

results.answer_markdown:
# MAU up 20% QoQ but revenue flat – root causes and actions

**Answer:** MAU rose 20% (12,466 → 14,888 monthly average) but net revenue fell 6.5% ($33.3k → $31.1k monthly average) because three independent drivers offset the volume gain: (1) the free daily episode limit was raised from 5 to 8 on 1 Sep, cannibalising ~$1.1k/mo of PPV standard revenue; (2) paid acquisition shifted from high-payer-rate channels (Meta, Google) to low-payer-rate channels (TikTok, influencer), dragging aggregate payer rate down 4.8 pp; (3) the US payer rate fell 4.8 pp (46.8% → 42.0%) on its own. New-market growth (PH, ID, BR, MX) added volume but at ¼ the US payer rate, amplifying the mix drag.

## What the numbers say
- **Q1 (Jun–Aug) vs Q2 (Sep–Nov) monthly averages** (Q1, Q2):
  - MAU: 12,466 → 14,888 (+19.4%)
  - Net revenue: $33,309 → $31,137 (−6.5%)
  - Payer rate: 28.3% → 23.5% (−4.8 pp)
  - ARPPU: $9.44 → $8.90 (−5.7%)
  - Revenue/MAU: $2.67 → $2.09 (−21.7%)

- **Free-limit change** (Q3, Q4, Q11): observed max free views/day jumped from 5 to 8 on 1 Sep. PPV standard views fell 64% (2,251 → 802/mo); PPV standard revenue fell 28% ($3,928 → $2,815/mo). 4,775–5,351 users/mo now consume the extra 3 free episodes.

- **Acquisition mix shift** (Q5, Q6, Q7): TikTok share of paid MAU rose 10% → 23% (payer rate 21% → 14%); Influencer 8% → 17% (20% → 14%). Meta fell 22% → 13% (41% → 43%); Google 21% → 11% (40% → 42%). Paid-channel spend shifted similarly (Q6).

- **US payer-rate decline** (Q8, Q23): US payer rate dropped steadily from 45.3% (Jun) to 41.9% (Nov) across *all* channels – not a mix shift. US MAU also slipped 3.5%.

- **New-market growth** (Q8, Q2, Q24): New-market MAU +56% (4,819 → 7,507) but payer rate fell 15.3% → 11.1%. They now contribute 50% of MAU but only 20% of revenue.

- **Data-quality note** (Q15): Refunds on Google Play in Oct–Nov are stored as positive amounts, inflating reported net revenue by ~$0.1k/mo in those months. The decomposition used `force_negative` to correct this.

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact (index pts on revenue, Q1=100) | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------------------------------------|------------|
| Free limit 5→8 (1 Sep) | PPV standard views −64%, PPV standard rev −28% | Q3, Q4, Q11, Q10 | −14.7 (rate step) | High |
| Paid-channel mix shift | TikTok 10%→23%, Influencer 8%→17% of paid MAU; both have ½ the payer rate of Meta/Google | Q5, Q6, Q7 | −13.97 (mix step) | High |
| US payer rate decline | 46.8%→42.0% across all US channels; US MAU −3.5% | Q8, Q23, Q2 | −8.38 (US rate step) | Medium |
| New-market volume at low monetisation | New-market MAU +56%, payer rate 15%→11% | Q8, Q2, Q24 | Captured in mix + rate steps | High |

## Bridge (index points, Q1 = 100)
| Step | Points | Cause |
|------|--------|-------|
| Start (Q1 monthly avg net revenue) | 100.0 | — |
| Volume (MAU +19.4%) | +19.43 | More users |
| Mix (segment shares) | −13.97 | Shift to new markets & low-payer-rate channels |
| Rate (payer rate within segments) | −14.70 | Free-limit cannibalisation + US payer-rate drop + new-market rate drop |
| Price (ARPPU incl. refunds) | +2.72 | Slightly higher ARPPU in US & some markets |
| **End (Q2 monthly avg net revenue)** | **93.48** | **−6.5%** |

Residual: 0.0 (decomposition accounts for all change).

## Ruled out
- **Price changes**: Subscription ($9.99) and PPV ($0.99/$1.99) list prices unchanged (Q16).
- **Refund surge**: Refund count fell 285→237/mo; refund amount turned positive in Oct–Nov only due to sign bug (Q10, Q15).
- **Charge failures**: Failure rates stable ~3–4% (Q18).
- **Content catalogue shift**: No evidence of premium/standard mix change in views.

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign bug on Google Play (Oct–Nov)**: 109+125 refund rows stored as positive, inflating net revenue by ~$0.1k/mo. Fixed in decomposition via `force_negative`. Engineering should correct the pipeline.
- **121 duplicate charge pairs** within 5 min (Q17) – low volume, monitor.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **A/B test free limit**: revert to 5 episodes for 50% of non-subscribers; measure PPV standard conversion, payer rate, retention at 30/60 days | Product / Growth | ~$1.1k/mo PPV revenue + potential sub uplift from tighter limit | PPV standard views/user, payer rate, D30 retention (guardrail) |
| **Reallocate paid spend**: shift budget from TikTok/influencer back to Meta/Google until CAC/payer parity; test creative to improve TikTok payer rate | UA / Marketing | $30k+/mo spend on channels delivering 14% payer rate vs 42% | Cost per payer by channel (30-day), payer rate by channel, ROAS |
| **Diagnose US payer-rate drop**: run survey + funnel analysis (paywall views → start trial → convert) by cohort; check if price sensitivity, content fatigue, or competitor promo | Product / Data | US = 65% of revenue; 4.8 pp drop = ~$2.9k/mo lost | Paywall view rate, trial start rate, conversion rate, NPS |
| **New-market monetisation playbook**: localise pricing (PPP), test lower sub price ($4.99), add carrier billing, improve premium content supply | Intl / Product | New markets = 50% MAU, 20% revenue; 4× revenue headroom | ARPPU by country, payer rate by country, revenue/MAU |
| **Fix refund sign pipeline** | Data Eng | Accurate revenue reporting, board trust | Zero sign violations in `amount_sign_by_type_method_month` check |

## Caveats and open questions
- **US payer-rate driver unknown** – no reason codes in data. Survey or qualitative research needed (Medium confidence it's not a mix artifact).
- **Free-limit A/B must guard retention** – the 3 extra free episodes may be retaining marginal users; measure D30/D60.
- **Cohort maturity**: Sep–Nov signups haven't completed full 30-day payer windows; Q2 payer rates will rise slightly as they mature.
- **Seasonality**: Only two quarters observed; cannot separate trend from seasonality.
